sections.h: More details on what you'll study.
t: Find out what you'll cover in this programme.

The programme fosters flexible collective learning. Throughout your studies, you’ll be supported by individual tutorials, group critiques, lectures, seminars and workshops, with critical feedback from world-leading contemporary artists, writers and curators. The curriculum is tailored to nurture the development of your art practice from the earliest manifestations of ideas to platforms for exhibition and making-public while providing the skills required to situate your practice within current material, technological and philosophical debates.

You will also learn from your fellow students, and they will learn from you. Each year a global cohort of students from diverse backgrounds, careers and life experiences joins our community. Peer-to-peer learning is a vital part of the RCA experience and this range of perspectives enriches students, igniting new ways of thinking and sparking innovation.
Outside of campus experience, you will have opportunities to explore London and immerse yourself in Europe's creative and cultural capital.
The programme is delivered across three terms and includes a combination of programme, School and College units. These will include:
Situating Contemporary Art Practice (45 credits)

This introductory unit provides the practical and theoretical foundations of the programme. A series of programme lectures, practical and generative workshops and seminars, individual tutorials and group sessions will support you in the production and experimentation of artworks, helping you to position and situate your practice within contemporary dialogues and debates.
Demonstrating Contemporary Art Practice (30 credits)

This unit engages with modes of making-public and with collaborative practices. You will have the opportunity to expand professional networks and engage with sites and contexts of art production and reception. You will be supported in your learning through individual and group tutorials, lectures, workshops and reading groups. You will also have the opportunity to collaborate with peers across all aspects of planning and delivery of a series of public projects and events which may involve external partners and also deliver a presentation of your work in the form of an artist Talk.

Also in Term 2, a choice of elective units will allow you to shape your own learning journey. You will have the opportunity to work alongside students from other programmes, bringing your practice into dialogue with the creative approaches of your peers. A full list of elective options will be published in 2027.
Independent Research Project (60 credits)

The Independent Research Project (IRP) is an opportunity to build a body of work that addresses the key ambitions of your research and practice. You will work towards presenting a work or works in the IRP Public Exhibition, which enables you to explore how you can activate your work in a public context, experiment with the most appropriate forms of realising your ideas and gain critical feedback. The IRP exhibition will be followed by a period of reflection and further development, which emphasises planning for continued practice and research post-graduation.

You will produce a final artwork for presentation in a public exhibition. You will be supported through individual and group tutorials and one-to-one technical support, alongside a series of programme-specific and School-wide professional practice lectures and workshops, with critical feedback on your work via an external group of arts professionals.
This MA is delivered over 45 weeks.

The Contemporary Art Practice MFA is an ambitious platform for research driven interdisciplinary artists. It creates an advanced critical and creative environment to further develop your independent study and helps to situate and articulate your practice in contemporary contexts. The programme is structured around evolving contemporary, critical questions, prompts and provocations. These inform the MFA programme activity and provide perspectives on the development of your study and research.

While we facilitate individual research outcomes, collective and collaborative working is at the core of the MFA. You will work with your peers to develop and stage a collaborative public outcome that reflects and builds on upon your own research interests but engages audiences in collective questions and concerns that have emerged from your study on the MFA.
In your first year, you undertake the same curriculum as our MA students, set out above, before extending your practice in your second year. Your second year will include:
Advanced Practice in Context (30 Credits)

This unit will support you in identifying an aspect of your practice as a focus for your MFA year enquiry; developing a systematic understanding of the relationship between process, context, and outcome. You will be introduced to practice-based research methods and debates to help you develop a proposal for your MFA Advanced Practice Portfolio and public outcome. Through the proposal process you will identify the conceptual significance, ethical demands and practical feasibility of your intended work. In addition to developing an individual proposal, you will work with the cohort to determine a set of critical questions and themes that will form the basis of your collective contribution to the discursive terrain of contemporary art.
Advanced Practice Portfolio (90 credits)

This unit is the culmination of the Master of Fine Art and is structured as an extended period of independent, practice-led enquiry in which you will realise a substantial and original body of work, critical research and reflection. A central aim of the unit is to support you in the development of an independent, authoritative and critical voice within your field of contemporary art and the ability to present your work to different audiences. Within the context of the MFA CAP, you will participate in shaping a critical discourse around art and its relationship to contemporary questions and debates. The culmination of the unit is the realisation and presentation of a resolved body of work as a part of a Show that is supported by appropriate forms of documentation and critical writing and reflection.
What you need to know before you apply

Candidates are selected entirely on merit and applications are welcomed from all over the world. The selection process considers creativity, imagination and innovation as demonstrated in your portfolio, as well as your potential to benefit from the programme and to achieve high Master's standards overall.

Candidates are generally expected to have a good BA degree from a fine art course. You should be able to demonstrate an original and critical approach to fine art as well as an ability to engage with current theories of art and culture that inform their practice.
Watch this video on how to make a good portfolio

We invite you to submit a curated selection of your recent practice. The examples can be in any media or form reflecting the multi-disciplinary nature of the Contemporary Art Practice Master's programmes.

All works may have a consistent form (e.g. a selection of photographic works) or be different. Video or sound work should be edited extracts no longer than five minutes each. Alongside the examples of your work, we would like you to describe how your work is situated within, or engages with, the histories/futures, theories and production of contemporary art.

Let us know what thinkers, writers and artists interest you and speculate upon why this is so. We would like to hear about your opinions and thoughts on global, social and political issues; in what way does your work and practice engage with crucial concerns – either personal and/or global?

Introduce us to your work and speculate on how your artworks address this or respond to it; this could be through the use of different processes, material choices, technologies, sites, interventions with groups or publics, critical writing, performance and the performative.
We are committed to decolonising the institutions of art and education; our current students work with a range of ideas regarding class, race, gender (feminism and trans) and disability.
Please provide a 300-word written personal statement that addresses the following points:
Introduce yourself, your interests and your motivations for applying to the Royal College of Art, and to this programme in particular.
Briefly summarise any educational background and professional experience to date that will support your application.
Tell us what you want to do in the future.
You must submit a video of no more than two minutes as part of the application process.

In the video, we want to hear why you want to study Contemporary Art Practice at the RCA. We encourage you to use this opportunity to situate your practice within the social, political and economic conditions of the contemporary world; identifying what art can contribute to ongoing material, critical, technological, and philosophical debates.

Discourse is a key aspect of 21st-century art production, and we expect you to be involved in navigating the relationship of art and the function of art's discourse for art's reception. In this two-minute video, please respond to the above statements and elaborate on the questions previously asked about your work and practice as documented in your portfolio.

sections.h: More details on what you'll study.
t: Find out what you'll cover in this programme.

The programme explores both the theory and practice of curating and programming. Through talks and lectures by visiting curators, readings, seminars and workshops, you will engage with topics informing contemporary curating, such as globalisation and migration, the digital and networked culture, urbanisation and use of space, and changing understandings of publics. Meanwhile, site visits offer insight into the complex and diverse range of spaces and places, galleries, museums and organisations in which curating and programming occurs.

You will learn to work collaboratively in peer groups on a live project brief set with an external partner. You will build skills in writing curatorial proposals, commission artists, designers and programmers and understand the role and value of project research and planning, presentation, mediation, and advocacy. In the final term, you will work in groups to curate a display of your project proposal and deliver a public-facing event, designed to generate audiences and critical debate.

You will also learn from your fellow students, and they will learn from you. Each year a global cohort of students from diverse backgrounds, careers and life experiences joins our community. Peer-to-peer learning is a vital part of the RCA experience and this range of perspectives enriches students, igniting new ways of thinking and sparking innovation.
Outside of campus experience, you will have opportunities to explore London and immerse yourself in Europe's creative and cultural capital.
The programme is delivered across three terms and includes a combination of programme, School and College units. These will include:
Curatorial Thinking (30 credits)

Curatorial Thinking introduces you to current and dominant positions and histories within curatorial studies, whilst exploring how the curatorial may be understood as a broader cultural phenomenon, as well as an approach to critically engaging with our contemporary moment. The aim of this unit is to develop your critical analytical skills, so you can establish your own understanding of what curating might mean as a practice, approach and way of thinking in and of our time. Taught through lectures, seminar discussion and the close reading of texts, assessed by a comparative textual analysis and thematic essay, the unit aims to develop your confidence in approaching theoretical texts and applying theory to the analysis of practice and vice versa.
Ecologies of Curating (15 credits)

Ecologies of Curating enables you to develop an understanding of the contemporary arts ecology, equipping you in the process with the skills to critically examine the inter-relation between curating, programming and the spaces and places in which contemporary art is generated, displayed, mediated and promoted. Focused on specific typologies of practice, organisations and platforms you will think through in groups how the conditions in which these exist determine and define what is produced and curated, and who for. The unit follows Curatorial Thinking, and is designed to develop your curatorial understanding of the relation between theory and practice through the realisation of a practice-based manifestation of your research generated in the unit and presented in a display of printed matter at the RCA.
Curating in a Collaborative Context (30 credits)

Curating in a Collaborative Context aims to develop your research-based and practice-orientated curatorial skills of analysis, conceptualisation and communication through collaborative, group project work. Responding to a specific project brief set by an external partner arts organisation, you will work with your peers to develop a curatorial proposal to Shortlist / Feasibility Stage of sector standards for presentation and feedback to your external partner. The unit follows the stages of proposal development from analysis of the project brief, research into context of the brief, identifying curatorial and programming opportunities towards commissioning, context analysis, audience projection, visualisation and documentation, presentation and advocacy.

Also in Term 2, a choice of elective units will allow you to shape your own learning journey. You will have the opportunity to work alongside students from other programmes, bringing your practice into dialogue with the creative approaches of your peers. A full list of elective options will be published in 2027.
Independent Research Project (60 credits)

The final unit provides you with the opportunity to curate a public display of a collaboratively created curatorial proposal and programme a public event that tests the ideas of the proposal. Aiming to extend your understanding of the relationship between critical reflection, practice and research, you will individually explore an element of your proposal through an extended piece of research.
This MA is delivered over 45 weeks.
“In recent years, CCA students have responded to briefs developed in collaboration with organisations as diverse as Artangel, Art Monthly, Chisenhale, Delfina and the Triangle Network.”
What you need to know before you apply

Candidates are selected entirely on merit and applications are welcomed from all over the world. The selection process will consider creativity, imagination and innovation as demonstrated in your portfolio, as well as your potential to benefit from the programme and to achieve high MA standards overall.

You are generally expected to have a good undergraduate degree from an arts or humanities background.If your undergraduate degree is not arts or humanities-based you should be able to articulate its relevance, or how it informs your aim to study Curating Contemporary Art. You also need to be able to demonstrate an active interest in contemporary art and its presentation and mediation, and have some practical experience of working within the visual arts or cultural sector that is relevant to the field of curatorial practice.

As a student on this programme you will help to develop the multi-, interdisciplinary and exploratory nature of contemporary curatorial practice and the future of curating. One of the primary aims of this programme is that you develop the skills and confidence to work effectively within this field, to act as an innovative and responsible practitioner, and that you contribute to the valuing of art and culture in your future work.
Watch this video on how to make a good portfolio
As part of your application, we want to learn what kinds of curatorial practice and contemporary art interest you. To do this, we ask you to upload two separate submissions:

Critical Review (500 words maximum) This text should offer a critical reflection and assessment of a contemporary art exhibition or project that you have recently visited. Tell us why you think it is successful or not in relation to its curatorial approach.

Curatorial Proposal You should upload a proposal for a contemporary art exhibition or project that you would like to curate. Tell us what the rationale behind your proposal is, what your curatorial approach would be (how will you curate), what artists/works/content would it include and where would you like it to take place.

You may wish to think about what audiences the project is for and if you will put together a public programme. The submission should be no more than four sides of A4 and include images as appropriate.
Please provide a 300-word written personal statement that addresses the following points:
Introduce yourself, your interests and your motivations for applying to the Royal College of Art, and to this programme in particular.
Briefly summarise any educational background and professional experience to date that will support your application.
Tell us what you want to do in the future.
You must submit a video of no more than two minutes as part of the application process.
This should include:
What kinds of questions, issues and experiences motivate your interests?
What role and value do you think curating brings to contemporary art?
Why do you want to join this particular programme?
At the core of the CCA programme is learning how to think, work and curate collaboratively so tell us why working collaboratively appeals to you rather than studying independently.

What experience do you have of team-working? This could be either in your academic experience, but it may also be in jobs you have had or voluntary work. Throughout your application, we’re interested in learning from you what motivates you and how you are building your knowledge and finally, what role and value this Master's represents for your future career.

Engage individuals in debate, develop alternative strategies and change minds and behaviours as a design futures practitioner. Working individually and with peers, we’ll encourage you to explore how design futures can address complex social and environmental challenges.

On the RCA Design Futures MA, you’ll develop a transdisciplinary approach to your design practice and strengthen your research methodology so you can refine your thinking. You might come to this programme with an established design practice that you want to push further; or from outside traditional design fields, but with a desire to integrate design tools into your work.

Become involved with projects that open new ways of thinking about design. Start bold conversations about the future. Embrace uncertainty and complexity. You’ll learn how to help people visualise alternatives and to make a positive response towards a more sustainable future.

Through your independent research project, you can focus on social and environmental challenges that matter to you. You’ll also develop your entrepreneurial skills for professional contexts and strategies for taking your ideas forward.
The Design Futures MA can be studied as a full-time or a part-time programme.

Flexibility and choice are at the heart of the offer, with a combination of Core and Elective units enabling you to create a bespoke programme of studies that best suits your approach, context and interests.

Units are delivered through a combination of lectures, seminars, and group tutorials, including in-person and online delivery. Concurrent units will be delivered through burst learning, with intense on-campus activity in blocks to provide a more sequential experience of the units. Between on-campus activity, online seminars, group tutorials and peer-led asynchronous activities support and structure your independent study.

You will be encouraged to engage with your network of peers and to collectively contribute to common learning resources, student-led seminars and peer critique. You are encouraged to treat your peers as critical friends, and to engage in critique in ways that are informed by your existing experiences of industry and practice. By participating in peer critiques, you will receive constructive feedback and learn to critique your work more effectively.
Opportunities for formative feedback are used to support and structure your learning. Peer and tutor critiques form an important part of the teaching, and occur in every unit.

You will also learn from your fellow students, and they will learn from you. Each year a global cohort of students from diverse backgrounds, careers and life experiences joins our community. Peer-to-peer learning is a vital part of the RCA experience and this range of perspectives enriches students, igniting new ways of thinking and sparking innovation.
Outside of campus experience, you will have opportunities to explore London and immerse yourself in Europe's creative and cultural capital.
The programme is delivered across three terms and includes a combination of programme, School and College units. These will include:

You'll begin by taking Research Methodologies (15 credits) , which introduces research and futures methodologies to support the imagination and realisation of alternative futures by engaging with diverse forms of knowledge, stakeholders and perspectives.

You’ll also take Complex Systems (15 credits), which introduces complexity, wicked problems, systems thinking, theories of change, and leverage points for design. Students develop an understanding of working with secondary data and qualitative insights to comprehend contexts, identify root causes, and find opportunities for transformation and value.

In term two you take Envisioning Futures , which combines futures methods with advanced digital and analogue envisioning methods bringing to life near and deep futures from a multi-species perspective.

You'll start to plan your Individual Research Project (IRP) Proposal (15 credits) by developing a research proposal to demonstrate the need for research on your chosen topic, articulate any gaps of knowledge and how your research proposal intends to address this.

Also in Term 2, a choice of elective units will allow you to shape your own learning journey. You will have the opportunity to work alongside students from other programmes, bringing your practice into dialogue with the creative approaches of your peers. This could either be through tackling ‘wicked’ design problems from a range of different perspectives, by collaborating on themed interdisciplinary projects, or by exploring how mutual exchanges of ideas and interpretations can foster a socially engaged practice. A full list of elective options will be published in 2027.
The final term is devoted to the development and realisation of your Independent Research Project (60 credits).

The independent research project (IRP) is the conclusion of your studies on the Design Futures MA. The independent research project is broken down into one 15 credit unit and a final 60 credit unit. The IRP is an opportunity for you to propose and realise a body of work that addresses the key ambitions of your research and professional practice. You will draw on what you have learnt on the programme to devise a project which might be individual or collaborative. You will also be encouraged and supported to identify opportunities for the professional public dissemination of your work. Your project will be supported through tutorials and opportunities to share your research developments through seminars and forums.
This MA is delivered over 45 weeks (full time) and 90 weeks (part time).
You will select electives to customise your own journey through the programme, choosing from a range of units offered by Design Futures and other programmes.
You'll be asked to rank your elective preferences and will be allocated based on those choices and availability. Elective offerings change each year.

The MA is delivered over 45 weeks (full time) and 90 weeks (part time). There are different periods of intensity in the programme. The first month is an intensive block for both full and part time students, then you will be on campus three to four days a week for full time and one to two days a week for part time.
What you need to know before you apply
Candidates are selected entirely on merit. We welcome applications from all over the world, as well as from mid-career designers and career changers.

The selection criteria considers creativity, imagination and innovation as demonstrated in your portfolio or equivalent professional experience, as well as your potential to benefit from the programme and to achieve the MA standard overall.

Students on the Design Futures programme will develop the role of Design within an interdisciplinary context to address global environmental, cultural and societal challenges. This means we are looking for students from a very diverse range of backgrounds from either design or any other disciplines or professions.

For your application we want you to compile a single illustrated document (PDF, maximum ten pages and project proposal) showing us a diverse range of projects from previous studies, professional work or self-initiated work and you must include a project proposal. This should show clearly through writing and images of your own work your interest in pursuing Design as an interdisciplinary field that seeks to address current and future challenges.

If you are currently a designer or design student, select a few of your most creative, original and ingenious pieces of work, including your process and decision making, the skills and tools used, as well as its purpose and final outcome. If you're not a designer or a student from a different discipline, don’t worry – show us how you’ve achieved excellence in your own field, communicate it in writing and/or visually, and make it personal, evidencing your unique creativity and how this might be relevant to Design. In both cases we are interested in how you think, what gets you excited, your desire to learn new skills, and your ability to build and grow ideas that contribute to the future of design and the planet.
Word count: 700 words
Font: Minimum 10pt
Format: Include at the end of your portfolio PDF

The project proposal (700 words) is an indicative statement about what you intend to explore as a Design Futures issue on the programme. It is recognised that this will change and develop while you are studying. We want to understand your interests, your particular angle on this topic, the context, and how you would approach it. Avoid generic statements about global issues.
It should follow this structure:
Proposed project title
What challenges or areas do you wish to critically appraise as a Design Futures issue? (150 words)

What is your connection to this topic? Why is it important to you? What research or work, if any, have you done on this topic already? What personal experience or perspective do you bring? (150 words)

What research or work has been done by others to address this area or field? How does your proposal relate to existing work and/or scholarly debate? (150 words plus references where relevant).to published sources and projects)

What research or work has been done by others to address this area or field? How does your proposal relate to existing work and/or scholarly debate? (150 words plus references to published sources and projects)
What types of outputs or impact do you hope to produce on the Design Futures programme? Think beyond traditional design deliverables. What change do you want to create? (150 words)
You may not submit links to external sites or materials.
The Royal College of Art supports interdisciplinary art and design practice and encourages applicants with diverse backgrounds and work experience.
Word count: 300 words
Address the following points:
Introduce yourself, your interests, and your motivations for applying to the RoyalCollege of Art, and to this programme in particular.
Briefly summarise any educational background and professional experience to date that will support your application.
Tell us what you want to do in the future.
To help your statement stand out, make sure to write this in your own voice.

Submit a short (two-minutes max length) video where you briefly introduce yourself and articulate what knowledge, skills and opportunities you think answers the question below. Use this opportunity to communicate your passions and personality. Avoid repeating what’s in the personal statement.
Answer the question: What does design futures mean to you?

Here are some prompts to help you answer this question: Consider not only RCA’s programme, but also the wider field of design futures. What drew you to this field? From your perspective, what does the practice of design futures look like? What is its potential in addressing complex societal and environmental challenges? Is there a particular area of design futures work that you would like to develop? You may wish to include examples from people whose work you admire and/or from your own portfolio.
Requirements
You must be visible in the video all the times.
You must communicate verbally yourself. Avoid reading your presentation as this makes it difficult for us to assess your presentation skills.
The video must be in real time (no speed adjustments).
Formats accepted: .avi, .mp4, .mov, .wmv
Please note, we are not judging you on your technical, production skills, but are using the video as an introduction to yourself and your aims for the programme.

The MArch Design Practice is a transformative one-year programme for architects, designers, spatial and creative practitioners at any career stage – whether you’re looking to reimagine an established practice, emerging from undergraduate study, or transitioning from other creative, activist or policy-engaged fields.

Planetary crisis demands new design thinking. This programme positions students at the intersection of urgent planetary challenges and unprecedented opportunity. You’ll study material processes and innovation, strategies of specification and reuse, embodied carbon and emerging technologies – from critically engaging AI and carbon accounting methods, developing interdisciplinary design strategies and methods of representation, to bio-based materials, and more. You’ll explore how these sites of opportunity intersect with economics, politics, and identity to reshape design practice.

We examine how renewable energy systems, green technologies, and social movements are transforming the built environment. Through critical engagement with construction's planetary impact, you'll develop bold, rigorous design propositions for more equitable futures, for people and planet.

Drawing on methods and theories from diverse international contexts, we prepare you to deliver renewable and equitable futures around the world. You'll bring your unique cultural perspective and existing practice into dialogue with peers from across the globe.

Students work across a range of media and contexts, including drawing, model-making, moving image, performance, material experimentation, prototyping, digital media, carbon accounting, policy engagement and design detailing.

This is not a RIBA/ARB validated Part II programme. Our structure offers flexibility for practitioners to tailor their learning to specific goals, whether you're working towards a specialism, developing a research-led practice, or pivoting your career. Students are encouraged to draw on existing practices and experiences, and to use the skills and exposure of the programme to propose interventions into existing architectural models or develop new forms of practice.

You'll take core units in the School of Architecture while choosing from interdisciplinary electives across the Royal College of Art – from digital storytelling to creative pedagogy, investigating the politics of housing, exploring sound design and new media, and more.

You'll develop an independent research project with dedicated one-to-one supervision, supported by intensive research workshops, career development sessions, and CV/application guidance to launch your next chapter. No two student journeys are identical. Each graduate is supported to carve out their own individual trajectory following their time with us on the programme.

This programme offers a rare opportunity: dedicated time and mentorship to analyse the crises facing the built environment and develop your own tools, methods, and practice models for engaging them. Whether you're two years or twenty years into your career, you'll graduate equipped to lead design toward just futures.

Flexibility and choice are at the heart of the offer, with a combination of Core and Elective units enabling you to create a bespoke programme of studies that best suits your approach, context and interests.
The programme's core units will be mainly delivered on campus, with some electives available online. Online resources will further contribute to students' learning. Units will include:

The part-time MA is delivered over 90 weeks.
Material Processes

This unit critically engages with the materiality of the built environment. The unit builds on physical, aesthetic and structural understandings of materials toward a deeper examination of their complex climatic, cultural, and political properties. The unit equips you with knowledge of wider implications and potential uses of material in architecture and design.
Carbon Economies

Through this unit, you will examine the role of carbon within a globalised building industry. You will explore methods of carbon modelling and accounting, campaigns for divestment and energy reform, and the potential of alternative, renewable energy sources to radically reconfigure practice. You will learn to analyse energy sources and evaluate the spatial implications of their use, and strategically position your practice at the forefront of technical and social changes.
Detailing Risk

The design detail is a site of connection and mediation between different aesthetic, legal, material, structural and energetic requirements. The failure of the detail creates risks that might imperil life or have adverse impacts on human health and well-being. This unit inverts the normative study of design detailing by turning to breakdowns and catastrophes where details, joints and connections have failed, because those failures illuminate problems that may have otherwise remained obscure or badly formulated. Drawing on forensic methods, you will learn to track the network of relations that radiate out from these moments of failure in order to better understand the role of detailing in the context of communal and social risk. Upending the typical design process, you will begin with final construction details and design through disassembly, ‘unbuilding’ failed details to understand their yield points and the underlying conditions of their catastrophic undoing.
Just Transition

This unit requires you to project into possible, just futures and rigorously develop the means of realising the transition to those futures. You will be exposed to the imaginaries, strategies and tactics of climate justice movements that contest and project beyond carbon, and consider the spatial implications of the ideologies and methods of these movements. You will critically engage the worlds these movements seek to bring about and consider how the skills and knowledge of spatial practitioners have a role to contribute in facilitating change. You will work across temporalities, producing Design Policy Proposals that can be implemented in the present that contribute towards operationalising renewable, just futures.
Independent Research Project

The Independent Research Project (IRP) unit comprises a substantial student-led investigation. You will be tutored towards the formulation of a research question, and supported to find appropriate and innovative research methods and documentation. You will be encouraged to draw on their existing contexts and/or develop new sites of practice towards making meaningful contributions to knowledge on climate and the built environment.

The MArch in Design Practice offers you the opportunity to engage the social and political systems underlying the climate crisis by design. You will be equipped to understand, analyse and contend with these systems and supported to develop propositions which seek to creatively and constructively bring about change.

You will also learn from your fellow students, and they will learn from you. Each year a global cohort of students from diverse backgrounds, careers and life experiences joins our community. Peer-to-peer learning is a vital part of the RCA experience and this range of perspectives enriches students, igniting new ways of thinking and sparking innovation.
Outside of campus experience, you will have opportunities to explore London and immerse yourself in Europe's creative and cultural capital.

What you need to know before you apply

The programme is aimed both at postgraduate students and mid-career professionals, and offers a balance between core knowledge, elective and collaborative work and a self-defined research project – enabling you to choose your own areas of interest, while developing the skills to implement your ideas.

Candidates are selected entirely on merit, and applications are welcomed from all over the world, as well as from mid-career designers and career changers. The selection criteria considers creativity, imagination and innovation as demonstrated in your portfolio or equivalent professional experience, as well as your potential to benefit from the programme and to achieve the MArch standard overall.

The programme welcomes architects, designers and spatial practitioners from a range of backgrounds, including those from other design disciplines such as sound, moving image or performance, with an interest in the built environment. Applicants from other backgrounds are also welcome, such as practitioners involved in local government, NGOs, journalism and activism.

Applicants from art, design and architectural backgrounds

Please submit a 10-page PDF portfolio that showcases your skills and motivations as an architect, artist and/or designer. Please include at least three projects you have worked on that are relevant to the programme. Clearly identify your contributions to any collective projects shown.

Please submit a 10-page PDF portfolio that showcases your skills and motivations as an artist and/or designer. Please include at least three different projects you have worked on, and clearly identify your contributions to any collective projects shown.
Applicants from non-portfolio disciplines (e.g. social sciences, sciences, humanities, politics, NGO/development work)
Please provide an illustrated 10-page document of previous work related to the MArch programme's themes. Clearly identify your role and contributions in the work.
Please provide a 300-word written personal statement that addresses the following points:
Introduce yourself, your interests and your motivations for applying to the Royal College of Art, and to this programme in particular.
Briefly summarise any educational background and professional experience to date that will support your application.
Tell us what you want to do in the future.

You must also submit a short video introducing yourself, how you envisage the programme will allow you to develop as a spatial practitioner, and what contributions it will support you to make in the world.

Identify opportunities rather than simply respond to problems , asking where design can contribute meaningfully and where established assumptions need to be challenged.

Products do more than meet needs. They embody assumptions about what matters, about who they are for, about how resources should be used to create and sustain them, and about what kinds of futures are possible through their creation. An object shapes a world.

At a time of rapid technological, ecological and social change, product design demands more than the ability to solve predefined problems. Designers need to recognise which questions are worth pursuing, and to make discerning decisions about how to do so under conditions of deep complexity and uncertainty.

sections.h: Design Products builds on a legacy of radical experimentation in product design
t: The Design Products MA/MDes programme asks you to explore what a product can be, what design can do, and where your own practice might lead. You might work through objects, materials and manufacturing, emerging technologies, digital and computational systems, experiences, services or interventions. Rather than prescribing a single definition of product design, we encourage you to develop a distinctive position of your own – grounded in research and sharpened through ambitious experimentation and critique.
The aim is not to produce one kind of designer. It is to help you develop a rigorous, adaptive practice capable of leading in a field whose boundaries are continually changing.

Design Products combines intellectual enquiry with material and practical experimentation. Throughout the programme, you will move between large questions and tangible interventions: researching complex contexts, testing ideas through prototypes and experiments, engaging with external expertise, and learning how design propositions change when they encounter people, materials, technologies and real-world conditions.

sections.h: Our understanding of impact is broader than the production of a successful object
t: A project might introduce a new material practice, make an overlooked relationship visible, challenge an established system, create new forms of interaction, open a new field of enquiry, or develop into a product, service, venture or independent practice.

You will study within a diverse international community of designers and practitioners and have opportunities to connect your work with expertise across the RCA and beyond. Design Products has a long history of producing designers whose practices have expanded the possibilities of the discipline, and we see that spirit of experimentation as central to its future.

Graduates take their work in many directions – from product and industrial design to materials, technology, research, entrepreneurship, interaction, strategic and speculative practice. Whatever direction you pursue, the programme is intended to cultivate designers who respond to uncertainty with curiosity and boldness, balanced with critical reflection and discernment.
Design Products can be taken as a one-year MA or a two-year MDes programme. MDes students follow the MA curriculum for year one before progressing to year two of the programme.

The second year of the MDes creates time and space to take the questions, practices and ambitions developed during the first year significantly further. In year two you will extend the direction established through your first-year Independent Research Project, building deeper expertise, relationships and experience within contexts relevant to your work. The emphasis shifts towards understanding the ecology required to sustain a practice: the collaborators, stakeholders, resources, knowledge, audiences and forms of value that allow ideas to develop beyond the College.
For full details of the MA and MDes curriculum view the Curriculum tab above.
Please make sure you apply for the programme you wish to study:
If you wish to study for the one year programme, please apply for the MA.
If you wish to study for the two year programme, please apply for the MDes.
There is no guaranteed progression from the MA to MDes and changing programme length may create challenges with student visas or finances.

sections.h: More details on what you'll study.
t: Find out what you'll cover in this programme.

You will learn through a range of teaching typologies in each unit including briefing, critique, exhibition, group tutorial, individual tutorial, lectures, seminars, demonstrations, workshops, peer reviews and independent study. Each unit will comprise of one or more projects which will develop learning up to the assessment point.

We will formally assess learning once in each unit with a formative and summative assessment. A critique or demonstration will be used for either the formative or summative assessment with asynchronous assessment methods including explanatory short video, desktop display, portfolio, visual presentation, and demonstration used for the other assessment point. The formative assessment will provide you with feedback on the strengths and weaknesses of their work-to-date and recommend strategies for improving learning to enhance the outcome of the summative assessment.

You will submit work in a range of both digital and physical formats depending on the unit project briefs. Examples of submission formats include writing, videos, 2D drawings, sketches and diagrams to test rigs, proof of principle, demonstrators, simulations, prototypes or models.

You will also learn from your fellow students, and they will learn from you. Each year a global cohort of students from diverse backgrounds, careers and life experiences joins our community. Peer-to-peer learning is a vital part of the RCA experience and this range of perspectives enriches students, igniting new ways of thinking and sparking innovation.
Outside of campus experience, you will have opportunities to explore London and immerse yourself in Europe's creative and cultural capital.

Design Products offers two routes: a one-year MA and a two-year MDes . Both begin with a common first year in which you develop an increasingly independent design practice through research, experimentation, making and critical reflection.

Throughout the programme, we ask you to think expansively about what a product can be, what it does, and the relationships and systems of which it becomes part . Products may be physical or digital, experimental or speculative; they may operate at the scale of an object, an interaction, a community or a wider system. What connects them is a commitment to exploring how design can engage critically and creatively with contemporary life.

You will work across materials, technologies, methods and contexts, learning through critical experimentation and collaboration. Rather than following a single model of product design, you will be encouraged to develop a distinctive practice of your own: one that is intellectually grounded, technically and creatively ambitious, attentive to its consequences, and capable of evolving as the world around it changes.
The first year moves through three broad stages: locating and expanding your practice; deepening and testing; and bringing this learning together through an independent research project.
These will include:

sections.h: Term 1: Locate and expand your practice
t: Your first term is a period of orientation, exploration and experimentation.

In Locating Practice , you will examine where your existing practice sits within a changing design landscape and consider where you want it to go. You will strengthen your research skills, identify areas for technical and intellectual development, and explore ways of connecting research with making. Through projects, proposals, probes and prototypes, you will develop ways to research, frame, test and communicate ideas through design.

Alongside this, Experimental Design encourages you to stretch the boundaries of your practice. Through fast-moving experiments and exploratory projects, you will work with different methods, materials and technologies and learn through iteration, testing and productive failure. Your experiments might be physical, digital, material, computational, biological or performative, and could take the form of products, artefacts, prototypes, interventions or propositions that challenge conventional definitions altogether.

The aim is not simply to produce more ideas, but to become a more adaptive and reflective designer : able to work with uncertainty, recognise unexpected possibilities and choose methods appropriate to the questions you are pursuing.
In the second term, the emphasis moves from expanding possibilities towards developing depth, position and responsibility.

Through Advanced Practice , you will deepen particular areas of your emerging practice and explore how design operates within larger social, technological, cultural and ecological contexts. Working collaboratively, you will use research, experimentation, prototypes and probes to investigate complex questions, engage with stakeholders and external expertise, and test not only whether an idea can work but what it might mean, whom it affects and what responsibilities it creates.

You will encounter knowledge and perspectives from beyond product design and be encouraged to engage with practitioners and disciplines such as engineering, science, architecture, anthropology and the arts. Through this process, you will begin to establish a more confident position of your own while learning how your practice relates to wider communities of knowledge and practice.

Also in Term 2, a choice of elective units will allow you to shape your own learning journey. You will have the opportunity to work alongside students from other programmes, bringing your practice into dialogue with the creative approaches of your peers. This could either be through tackling ‘wicked’ design problems from a range of different perspectives, by collaborating on themed interdisciplinary projects, or by exploring how mutual exchanges of ideas and interpretations can foster a socially engaged practice. A full list of elective options will be published in 2027.

By the end of the term, the different strands of the year begin to converge: the questions you care about, the methods you have developed, the materials and technologies you work with, and the kind of designer you are becoming.
The Independent Research Project (IRP) is the culmination of the first year.

Here, you take increasing ownership of an ambitious project that brings together the research, experimentation, making and critical thinking developed throughout the programme. Rather than responding to a tightly prescribed brief, you define and pursue a design question of your own and determine the methods, collaborations and forms through which it can best be explored.

The mode of learning consequently shifts towards supervision and independent practice. You will spend much of your time developing and making your work, supported by strategic academic supervision and negotiated technical support.

The IRP is an opportunity to demonstrate the position that drives your practice: what you believe design can contribute, how your work relates to contemporary practice, and what new territory your project might open.
Your project culminates in public presentation and exhibition, creating an opportunity to communicate your work, encounter responses to it and reflect on what you have learned.

For MA students, this completes an intensive 45-week programme and provides a foundation from which to take your developing practice into professional, entrepreneurial, research or further creative contexts.
For students taking the two-year MDes route, Year 2 creates time and space to take the questions, practices and ambitions developed during the first year significantly further.
Where Year 1 culminates in an independent project, Year 2 asks a different question: how might that work develop into a sustained practice capable of operating in the world?

You will extend the direction established through your Independent Research Project, building deeper expertise, relationships and experience within the contexts relevant to your work. Depending on your practice, these might include industry and manufacturing, research, cultural organisations, communities, emerging technologies, entrepreneurship or other professional and public contexts.

In the second year, the emphasis shifts from developing an individual project, towards understanding the ecology required to sustain a practice: the collaborators, stakeholders, resources, knowledge, audiences and forms of value that allow ideas to develop beyond the College.

sections.h: Term 4: Build the conditions for practice
t: Through Professional Development & Contextual Framing , you will explore the professional and wider context in which your practice could develop.

You will identify and build relationships with relevant collaborators, organisations, clients, stakeholders, facilities and other forms of expertise, learning to negotiate the practical conditions through which ambitious design work becomes possible.

Professional development here is understood broadly. For some students this may involve establishing a studio or commercial proposition; for others it may mean developing a research-led, socially engaged, technological or collaborative practice.
The aim is to move beyond thinking about a project in isolation and begin building the network of relationships through which your practice can have agency and impact.

sections.h: Terms 5 and 6: Develop and test a sustained practice
t: During the MDes Major Project , you will put this developing practice into action.

Working increasingly beyond the immediate environment of the programme, you will draw upon the relationships and contexts established during the previous term to develop, test and refine your work. You will learn through the realities of collaboration and professional engagement: negotiating different interests, responding to constraints, adapting your ideas and understanding how value is created and communicated within your chosen field.

Success is not defined simply by establishing a fully sustainable practice within the year. The emphasis is also on the learning and development involved in trying to make a practice viable – understanding what works, what changes when ideas encounter real contexts, and how your practice might continue to evolve beyond the RCA.
The two-year MDes is delivered over 90 weeks, comprising 45 weeks of study in each year.

What you need to know before you apply

Candidates are selected entirely on merit and applications are welcomed from all over the world. The selection process considers creativity, imagination and innovation as demonstrated in your portfolio, as well as your potential to benefit from the programme and to achieve high Master's standards overall.

For Design Products, you should have a good undergraduate degree or equivalent in an area of design, or related background and proficient written and spoken English. Several years of professional experience, either before or after a first degree, is a benefit, and you must be able to demonstrate critical and innovative thinking, a design curiosity and the ability to thrive in student led projects.

Applications are welcomed from candidates from related backgrounds, such as engineering, architecture, communication, sports science, medical/health, international development/NGO, economics/business, material science, technology development and user experience.

We are looking for people from all backgrounds who are interested in using design to solve problems and enrich lives. Use your portfolio to highlight your work and skills. We especially want to understand your thinking process, how to you frame problems and tackle them, how you measure success and learn from challenges.
Portfolio (required)
We want to see the depth and quality of your work, especially your approach to design work, interests, and ambitions.
Pick your best projects to include that highlight your technical skills and design thinking process.
Communicate the story of each project: the motivations, specific design problems, how you solved them, what you learned through testing/iteration
Highlight challenges or failures and how they were addressed
Works in progress may be included
Works that has been deployed in public (to real-world/places/people) is especially valuable
Clearly identify your role and specific contributions when including group projects
Any kind of project is acceptable. Even from a non 'design' field, tell us about it as outlined above
Research/Project agenda (required)
Tell us about your specific research plans. What is your area of interest within the field of design and what types of problems do you want to pursue while in the programme?
It should be:
600–800 words, submitted in pdf format
Propose a research question that you are interested in exploring through the Design Products programme
Define your motivation and the significance (i.e., what is the potential benefit) of the problem you would like to investigate
Provide some referenced background describing how the problem is grounded in the field of design (i.e., what has been done in the past and why the issue you are interested in currently exists)
Your Interests (optional)
Tell us about any other interests or activities you take part in: anything else that informs your interests, how you view the world, and helps to enrich your process and learning.
Do you:
work in a lab, maker space, or participate in a technical club/group?
collect interesting things?
travel extensively?
regularly visit exhibitions/museums?
Please provide a 300-word written personal statement that addresses the following points:
Introduce yourself, your interests and your motivations for applying to the Royal College of Art, and to this programme in particular.
Briefly summarise any educational background and professional experience to date that will support your application.
Tell us what you want to do in the future.
You must submit a video of no more than two minutes as part of the application process.
We would like you to pick a ‘designed work’ and create a video reflecting on:
how was it successful or influential
what are the positive and negative attributes about how it was used/applied
how would you improve or re-do the design if you could
This can be an example of your own work or something in the public domain. Use this to articulate your view on the role that design can play in impacting the world

Our programme will equip you to be a creative thinker, maker and leader in your chosen field. Our graduates work across the arts, design, technology, journalism, film, media and performance, establishing creative studios, contributing to industrial and public organisations, or pursuing advanced research and teaching in the evolving contexts, methodologies and applications of inclusive, immersive and interactive digital narrative practice.
Instagram
Learn to view the world critically, cutting through hype and misinformation.
Collaborate with others to explore how digital narrative arts and immersive, interactive storytelling can create positive and enduring change.
Shape the future of narrative and storytelling, working creatively and critically with emerging technologies as part of a world-leading community of researchers and practitioners.
Engage sensitively with diverse traditions and cultures, building an understanding of ethical and equitable narrative practice, and critical and analytical approaches to technology.

Evolving from the RCA’s Digital Direction MA programme, Digital Narrative Arts MA/MFA is a collaborative, interdisciplinary community exploring new approaches to narrative practice and global storytelling through emerging technologies. We create immersive, interactive, digital and generative narrative experiences, including art, games, film, sound, and live performance, combining research and experimentation with collective practice to rethink how contemporary digital narratives are shaped, shared and experienced. We work creatively and critically with artificial intelligence (AI), extended reality (XR), including game engines, virtual and augmented reality and real-time 3D, advanced sensing, physical computing and mobile platforms.

Developing diverse narrative logics, structures, ways of making and disseminating meaning, we create new possibilities for what narrative and storytelling can be; and explore how they can operate as critical tools for addressing social and ecological challenges, as a means for creating fairer and more sustainable futures. Join us to research knowledge systems and paradigms, and explore ways of working with people and other species to develop equitable planetary storytelling for real-world contexts.
Digital Narrative Arts can be taken as a one-year MA or a two-year MFA programme . MFA students follow the MA curriculum for year one before progressing to year two of the programme.

The MFA is for students who want to further develop and test new ways of applying advanced knowledge and skills in justice- and community-led, sustainable and global narrative practice with a wide range of partners and in real-world settings. It develops creative leadership in digital narrative arts, enabling students to experiment with new forms, knowledge, roles and technologies for immersive and interactive storytelling.
For full details of the MA and MFA curriculum view the Curriculum tab above.

Both programmes are transdisciplinary in nature and open to practitioners from the arts as well as designers, journalists, writers, musicians, theatre makers, performers, scientists, engineers, cultural practitioners and anyone who wants to experiment with new narrative concepts, environments, partnerships, formats and technologies driven by ethical, environmental, epistemological and social imperatives.
Digital Narrative Arts MA/MFA will be delivered at our Battersea campus for 2027/28. Find out more.

sections.h: More details on what you'll study.
t: Find out what you'll cover on this programme.
The MA programme is delivered across three terms, while the MFA is delivered over 6 terms. They feature a combination of programme, School and College units. These will include:

The Digital Narrative Arts MA programme provides a comprehensive, research-led platform for digital narrative practice, focused on knowledge and skills for developing and presenting compelling immersive and interactive narrative experiences that address urgent concerns in contemporary culture. Drawing sensitively from diverse storytelling and narrative practices, traditions and cultures, the programme encourages students to work with others to rethink and reframe what storytelling can be and how it can be combined responsibly with emerging technologies such as AI, XR and spatial computing.

During Critical Stories (60 credits), we will explore the foundational approaches of the programme, focusing on critical, co-operative and experimental storytelling methods, media ecologies and artefacts. During the unit you will be introduced to diverse concepts and practices relevant to contemporary storytelling, media and communication. Working with others, you will be asked to explore emerging critical directions for digital storytelling practice; iteratively design a technical approach that applies digital storytelling technologies through creative and cooperative practice; and work with and in consideration of others to explore an urgent context in contemporary culture.

Immersive Enquiries (45 credits) focuses on working critically and experimentally with immersive environments (not restricted to VR headsets), mobile platforms, and emerging areas of media practice to conceptualise, test and evaluate future directions. During the unit you will be asked to investigate urgent contexts and new approaches for immersive, real-world, digital storytelling; produce experimental content for extended reality contexts using relevant technical approaches; and work cooperatively with others to map the societal and environmental effects of your practice.

Also in Term 2, a choice of elective units will allow you to shape your own learning journey. You will have the opportunity to work alongside students from other programmes, bringing your practice into dialogue with the creative approaches of your peers. This could either be through tackling "wicked problems" from a range of different perspectives, by collaborating on themed interdisciplinary projects, or by exploring how mutual exchanges of ideas and interpretations can foster a socially engaged practice. A full list of elective options will be published in 2027.

In the Independent Research Project (IRP) (60 credits), you will have the opportunity to work independently to develop a comprehensive programme of research-led practice, critically exploring a topic of your own choosing through individual or collaborative approaches. The unit provides scope for you to bring together the core competencies, methods and processes you have developed during the programme and to define, contextualise, produce and evaluate a substantial body of creative and critical research. During the unit you will be asked to devise, direct and produce an ambitious programme of creative research that critically and inclusively assesses a contemporary real-world digital storytelling concern. You will also be asked to apply ethical forms of professionalism and production within your practice; and to identify relevant audiences for your work, including outside your immediate network, and to develop and evaluate your practice with them. Through your research you will also be asked to show how your practice contributes to debates that are at the forefront of the field.
This MA is delivered over 45 weeks.

Building directly on the MA, the MFA is for students who want to further develop and test new ways of applying advanced knowledge and skills in justice- and community-led, sustainable and global narrative practice with a wider range of partners and in real-world settings.

The MFA focuses on developing creative leadership in digital narrative arts, enabling students to experiment with new forms, knowledge, roles and technologies for immersive and interactive storytelling in creative practice, collective learning, research, policy, strategy and/or other responsible forms of innovation. This could take the form of leading a research project that could grow into an advanced research proposal; leading the development of new forms of narrative experiences; leading a collective or planning and developing a creative studio; or leading new applications for digital narratives in policy or related areas of practice.

Collective and collaborative learning is at the centre of the MFA, with students developing independently structured study approaches in conjunction with relevant audiences and organisations. Drawing from the RCA’s vibrant environment for research and innovation, these could include the RCA Immersive Acts Group, which provides a focus for the college’s immersive and interactive creative technology research, as well as the programme’s research and creative and cultural networks and industry partners.

During Advanced Practice in Context you will evolve your practice as a site of enquiry, developing a systematic understanding of relationships between concepts, processes, contexts, and outcomes. Through a combination of studio-based activity, working on location and with communities, critical reflection, and engagement with relevant disciplinary frameworks, you will refine your approach and develop a coherent research trajectory. By the end of the unit, you will be expected to demonstrate a clear and ambitious proposal for your MFA Advanced Practice Portfolio, evidencing both the conceptual grounding and practical feasibility of your intended work.

In the MFA Advanced Practice Portfolio , you will develop and realise a major, self-directed body of work. The unit is intentionally open in its structure, allowing for a wide range of approaches, media and outcomes, while maintaining a clear expectation of depth, rigour and coherence. You will be required to take full responsibility for the direction and management of your project, including the formulation of objectives, the selection and application of methods, and the organisation of your time and resources.

You will also learn from your fellow students, and they will learn from you. Each year a global cohort of students from diverse backgrounds, careers and life experiences joins our community. Peer-to-peer learning is a vital part of the RCA experience and this range of perspectives enriches students, igniting new ways of thinking and sparking innovation.
Outside of campus experience, you will have opportunities to explore London and immerse yourself in Europe's creative and cultural capital.

What you need to know before you apply

Candidates are selected entirely on merit and applications are welcomed from all over the world. The selection process considers creativity, imagination and innovation as demonstrated in your portfolio, as well as your potential to benefit from the programme and to achieve high MA/MFA standards overall.

You will normally have completed an undergraduate qualification in a relevant subject or be able to evidence equivalent professional experience in fields such as filmmaking, broadcasting, media and communication, fine art, graphic design, sound, music, illustration, theatre, writing, HCI or digital production.
All candidates are required to submit an online portfolio of work to be assessed by the programme team; see below for more detail.

Candidates are selected on the basis of a body of work that demonstrates an advanced understanding of the subject and sufficient technical skill to realise intentions, evidence of commitment to the subject, intellectual curiosity, open-mindedness, the ability to collaborate, to engage in debate and respond to criticism, and the ability to engage in sustained and consistent study. We also look for enthusiasm for your practice and a strong sense of personal responsibility for your own learning and development.

Digital Narrative Arts addresses our urgent need for inclusive and relevant storytelling, examining the emergence of new technologies and time-based media (which means media that change over time, such as video, sound, immersive environments, mobile platforms, VR, AR, games etc) alongside the future of storytelling itself. The programme is for creative and critical practitioners with diverse backgrounds who want to experiment creatively and collectively with new narrative approaches driven by ethical, environmental, epistemological and social imperatives, and who have a passion for exploring how storytelling can inform positive change.

Please submit one PDF portfolio containing documentation of no more than three projects or pieces of work that evidence your match and potential for meeting the aims of our course. We expect to see evidence of great interest in using technology to push the boundaries of storytelling, as well as the ability to bring a critical perspective to the hype surrounding such technologies.

Please include a separate section within the PDF portfolio for each of your projects or pieces of work. If any of your projects or pieces of work involve collaboration, please clearly describe your individual contribution to the project or piece of work. We advise you to include one page on research, one page on project development, one page on outcome(s), and one page on testing and evaluation, for each of the projects or pieces of work in your PDF portfolio. Please ensure that all text in your PDF portfolio is minimum font size 11. PDF portfolios should be no more than 100MB and format your portfolio for screen (approx 16:9).

Please also upload any media files that relate to your three projects or pieces of work using the spaces provided in the application system. Please label each of your media files clearly so that we can understand how they relate to your PDF portfolio. Suggested naming format: Title of Project or Piece of Work, Name of Media File (for example: Whale Fall, 3D Animated Video).
We welcome career changers. If you do not have a technical or time-based media or storytelling background, please also explain how and why you want to expand your work into these areas.
Please provide a 300-word written personal statement that addresses the following points:
Introduce yourself, your interests and your motivations for applying to the Royal College of Art, and to this programme in particular.
Briefly summarise any educational background and professional experience to date that will support your application.
Tell us what you want to do in the future.
You must submit a video of no more than two minutes as part of the application process.
In this video, please tell us why you want to join the programme:
What stories do you want to tell?
What ambitions do you have for your work?
How can technology specifically enhance the stories you want to tell?
What critical and conceptual perspectives will you bring to your studies?
Which theoretical or philosophical ideas and texts have advanced your understanding of storytelling, media and technology today?
What ideas interest you and why?

As well up uploading the above portfolio, statement and video, MFA applicants should additionally upload a short written proposal of no more than two pages setting out your initial ideas and intentions for the MFA second year, as well as the specific context(s) to which your proposed MFA studies relate.

If you are not a national of a majority English-speaking country you will need the equivalent of an IELTS Academic or UKVI score of 6.5 overall (with a minimum of 5.5 in every component). Students achieving a grade of at least 6.0, with a grade of 5.5 in the Test of Written English, may be eligible to take the College’s English for Academic Purposes course to enable them to reach the required standard.
You are exempt from this requirement if you have received a 2.1 degree or above from a university in a majority English-speaking nation within the last five years.
If you need a Student Visa to study at the RCA, you will also need to meet the Home Office’s minimum requirements for entry clearance.
Fees for September 2027 entry on this programme are outlined below. From 2021 onward, EU students are classified as Overseas for tuition fee purposes.
New entrants to the College will be required to pay a non-refundable deposit in order to secure their place. This will be offset against the tuition fees. Deposits for 2027 entry can be found below.

For alumni who have completed an RCA Graduate Diploma and progress onto an RCA Master's programme, a progression discount of £1,000 is available. For alumni progressing from an RCA Master's to another RCA Master's, a progression discount of £2,000 is available (£1,000 per year for part-time programmes).

Even if you do not currently see a scholarship for which you meet the eligibility criteria, we encourage you to apply to be considered for financial support.

Unless otherwise stated, you must apply in either round 1 or 2, and have received an offer of study on an RCA programme to be invited to make a scholarship application. Therefore, we strongly recommend you apply for your programme as early as possible but no later than the round 2 deadline.

In addition to your programme fees, please be aware that you may incur other additional costs associated with your study during your time at RCA. Additional costs can include purchases and services (without limitation): costs related to the purchase of books, paints, textiles, wood, metal, plastics and/or other materials in connection with your programme, services related to the use of printing and photocopying, lasercutting, 3D printing and CNC. Costs related to attending compulsory field trips, joining student and sport societies, and your Convocation (graduation) ceremony.

If you wish to find out more about what type of additional costs you may incur while studying on your programme, please contact the Head of your Programme to discuss or ask at an online or in person Open Day .

We provide the RCASHOP online, and at our Kensington and Battersea Campuses – this is open to students and staff of the Royal College of Art only to provide paid for materials to support your studies.
We also provide support to our students who require financial assistance whilst studying, including a dedicated Materials Fund.

There are many funding sources, with some students securing scholarships and others saving money from working. It is impossible to list all the potential funding sources; however, the following information could be useful.
Tuition fees are due on the first day of the academic year and students are sent an invoice prior to beginning their studies. Payments can be made in advance, on registration or in two instalments.

Environmental Architecture & Urban Design graduates are expected to go to work in a range of fields, from design agencies including architecture, landscape architecture and urban design and planning, to roles in the public sector and NGOs, and further academic study.

Environments across the world are transforming at a remarkable speed. Prolonged heat and drought are followed by intense rainfall and flooding; changing climates reshape how we live, move, source energy and share habitats. At the same time, technological and social change is transforming how we work, relate, and care for one another. Established distinctions between architecture, landscape architecture, urban design and environmental practice are increasingly inadequate for engaging with these interconnected conditions.

The Environmental Architecture & Urban Design MA brings these fields into productive dialogue, exploring how design can engage with the ecological, social, and political processes shaping contemporary life. Through design-action research, studio practice, and fieldwork, you’ll work across disciplines and scales to understand complex environments, develop forms of intervention, and define your own position within an expanding field of spatial practice.

The programme understands spatial change as inseparable from questions of organisation and collective life. New spatial arrangements – and new uses of existing ones – can require new forms of stewardship, governance and participation. You’ll explore how design can contribute not only to different environments, but to different relationships between people, institutions and the more-than-human worlds they inhabit.
Bring environmental thinking and urban design into productive dialogue.
Work with communities and institutions on urgent environmental, spatial and urban challenges.
Connect transformative design approaches with policy, fieldwork and speculation to enact change.
Develop your design practice within the justice-oriented, experimental, collaborative, and interdisciplinary culture of the RCA.

This programme is for students interested in the themes previously explored through the Environmental Architecture MA and City Design MA programmes, bringing together environmental, architectural and urban design approaches to address the challenges facing our cities and environments.
